pull.title: refactor: test: Unroll `&&` conditions in macros
pull.body:
Picked from #35713. Given that I think this is a strict debugging improvement, I opened as a separate pull:

Using `&&` in `BOOST_CHECK` is problematic as failures will not indicate which condition failed. By unrolling these checks, the user knows exactly which expression is the failing case.

As an example, here is a line that would be particularly hard to debug if it failed:

```
src/test/net_tests.cpp

BOOST_CHECK((*ret)[1] && (*ret)[1]->m_type == "headers" && std::ranges::equal((*ret)[1]->m_recv, MakeByteSpan(msg_data_2)));
```

If any one of these conditions fail, the whole expression fails, with no values printed or indication as to which condition failed.

This is also required when using test macros that support value decomposition, which requires `&&` and `||` are `delete`. Examples include `BOOST_TEST`, doctest, Catch2, etc.

ref: https://catch2-temp.readthedocs.io/en/latest/assertions.html#other-limitations
ref: https://fekir.info/post/decomposing-an-expression/

It is worth noting that breaking the chaining checks has behaviour changes,
There are instances where the execution of invariants depends on some being succeeding; that's why we are seeing the U.B's. 
I see some are guarded using require.

I don't know how much we worry about that, but I did a quick scan and didn't find more apart from ones spotted before.

If we are going to do this and make this a rule, maybe add a lint job that may see and warn against chaining, as is now, nothing will prevent adding the chaining now. You may either have to review all PR before they are merged or do some unrolling again later.

> or do some unrolling again later.

I'd say it should be rare enough to do another unroll later, if there is need to.

I'm not going to block the PR, but I disagree with many examples here - and it invalidates a lot of other PRs.
Some of the conditions make sense in groups - the author of the change should decide that, this just seems a more noisy way to express the same.
Sure, on failure it may make debugging easier, but it can also make the code harder to read by pushing everything to the foreground.

> Some of the conditions make sense in groups

The options:

* Give up on the idea of the single `TEST` macro
* Group the groups explicitly with double-braces: `TEST( ( a && b ) )`
* Something else?

> Sure, on failure it may make debugging easier

This is exactly the point of the pull. Why would we waste developer time by having them find which of the `N` conditions failed when it is logically equivalent to `N` independent checks? Saving time debugging should be the default, and if you insist on omitting the useful debug output and grouping conditions together, you may wrap the `&&` conditions in `( ... )` as was suggested above.

> can also make the code harder to read

This is subjective. Personally I find:
```
 BOOST_CHECK(s.command_line_options.contains("a") && s.command_line_options.contains("b") && s.command_line_options.contains("ccc")
                    && !s.command_line_options.contains("f") && !s.command_line_options.contains("d"));
```
difficult to read.

> Why would we waste developer time by having them find which of the `N` conditions failed

Sure, but the opposite also applies: why would we waste developer time by separating groups of conditions? The S/N ratio matters for readability, and when conditions are logically connected it can make sense to represent them as such in code.
> Personally I find:
>  BOOST_CHECK(s.command_line_options.contains("a") && s.command_line_options.contains("b") && s.command_line_options.contains("ccc")
>                     && !s.command_line_options.contains("f") && !s.command_line_options.contains("d"));
> difficult to read.

Yes, this definitely needs to go (e.g. a for loop could fix it), but this isn't the example I gave, but:
```C++
BOOST_CHECK(node->second.IsDirty() && !node->second.IsFresh());
```
and
```C++
BOOST_CHECK(flushed && state.IsValid());
```
where most people just skipped `state` validation since adding yet another assertion line seemed too noisy.

> you may wrap the && conditions in ( ... ) as was suggested above.

Yes, or immediately invoked lambda expressions probably work also.

> Suppose this condition failed

If this failed, it's because of something the developer *just* changed.
They can just unroll locally, rerun the test and check - like you mentioned, it's trivial, takes 10 seconds - we do it all the time. Outside of that narrow window everyone else has to parse several lines if we split, so the minority use case (failure caused by my local change) is prioritized over the majority case (people running passing tests and reading code).

> This pull request is not preventing the style you propose either

Yes, so let's split only the conditions like you mentioned, which obviously shouldn't be in the same line - without touching conflicting lines that invalidate other long-standing PRs, just to make something subjectively pretty in a theoretical and unlikely case.
Ping me for a review if you do that, but in its current form I'm not enthusiastic about this change. I won't block it, but I don't like that we're narrowing the ways we can express ourselves to have the tests reflect the intent.

Not sure how to proceed here. Maybe the controversial line `BOOST_CHECK(!flushed && state.IsError());` can be backed out for now and the main pull can change it to `BOOST_CHECK((!flushed && state.IsError()));` or something else?

Also, it looks like the UB from the thread https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35729#discussion_r3587683334 can be removed?

>  Maybe the controversial line BOOST_CHECK(!flushed && state.IsError()); can be backed out for now

This was in a pending pull, but I can get rid of `src/test/coinscachepair_tests.cpp` changes so we can try to move on with this.

only change is removing a UB risk and dropping changes in one file.

>  but I can get rid of src/test/coinscachepair_tests.cpp changes so we can try to move on with this.

At the risk of [bike shedding](https://bikeshed.com/) this even more, I don't think this achieves anything meaningful. If the subsequent PR disallows evaluating && in the check, it seems ideal to me to merge all the unrolling changes in one pull. This seems to me like punting some unrolling to another pull, I would rather we get them all at once, and the subsequent PR can just unroll newly added ones.

> I would rather we get them all at once

My argument here was exactly that not all combined checks are "bugs" - some things are just checked as belts-and-suspenders, just to be sure, but if we're forcing this rule that each assert should only contain a single check, I personally will just leave those extra checks out since most of those checks don't deserve a separate line.
The test becomes harder to read while it doesn't contribute meaningfully to its reliability. But if they're just added in the same line since we don't ever expect them to fail, and when they do, it does deserve our extra attention since likely our local modifications have broken it.

> My argument here was exactly that not all combined checks are "bugs"

I did not state they were bugs, not sure why that word is in quotes. The first sentence of the PR description is "I think this is a strict debugging improvement."

> some things are just checked as belts-and-suspenders, just to be sure

This is an ambiguous sentence. What does a belt and suspenders have to do with this?
 
e8691056c0140f8fa850fc6837dde915ebeb22cc reintroduces the `src/test/coinscachepair_tests.cpp` changes. This pull request should be evaluated on the basis that all `&&` may be separated into two individual checks, which I find useful for debugging and readability. Trying to develop exceptions to that rule is pointless and a waste of time. If developers prefer in-lining `&&` checks in a single macro, #35713 may be updated to reflect that preference.

Only change is restoring the version from 3 weeks ago (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35729#issuecomment-4991597167), plus one hunk to remove one possible UB.


</details>


No strong opinion on the style discussion, but I think it would help if people with a preference clearly stated what their preference is. Otherwise, the feedback is hard to understand and not really actionable.

For example,

* if the preference was to not work toward a unified test macro, the statement could be something like: "I don't think it is worth it to move toward a unified test macro, so my preference would be to just go with b8febd12966c8303e2ee6db91b9646717421ebd6 and change https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35713 to include individual/specific macros only."
* if the preference was to work toward a unified test macro, but use a different style for some check calls, the statement could be something like: "My preference would be b8febd12966c8303e2ee6db91b9646717421ebd6 and to use $style for the other cases, and then move forward normally with #35713".
* ...?

>  Trying to develop exceptions to that rule is pointless and a waste of time

Why do you think you need to introduce a new rule in the first place? The existing cases were done deliberately - some were well designed, others might not be, but calling everyone's work pointless and trying to force your preference seems a bit off...

> Why do you think you need to introduce a new rule in the first place?

The rule would be enforced by the compiler in #35713, which I tried to develop a workaround for, but was not satisfied with the tradeoff. Modern C++ test frameworks have this compiler level restriction, including catch2, doc test and `BOOST_TEST` itself, which I detailed in an earlier comment and the commit message. In addition to that restriction, I felt this was also a debugging improvement. I will reiterate the first sentence of this PR description, "I think this is a strict debugging improvement." This is why I have decided to open this as a separate pull. I am not just conjuring up rules as this comment implies.

> calling everyone's work pointless

Nowhere in the comment above did I call anyone's work pointless. I attempted to appease your feedback by removing the callsites that you left review on by creating an _exception_ to the rest of the changes in this pull. The response was unactionable feedback, with no direction as to what sites should and should not unroll && conditions. Therefore, I simply added these callsites back and concluded this change should be atomic with no exceptions.

I would appreciate if you refrained from using accusatory language when leaving review comments.

comments.body:
seems fine, but I wonder what the difference is between BOOST_REQUIRE and `Assert`.

There are already a few tests that use Assert:

```sh
git grep 'Assert(' ./src/test/*.cpp
```

Also, It is shorter to write either:

```cpp
        const CService gateway_ipv6{*Assert(Lookup("2a10:1234:5678:9abc:def0:0000:0000:0000", 1, false))};
```

or:

```cpp
        default_local_ipv6 = *Assert(local_ipv6);
```

than to use the BOOST_REQUIRE.


So my preference would be to move toward `Assert` where it makes sense, to avoid bloating the tests, but this seems also acceptable as-is.

I count around ~36 `BOOST_REQUIRE` in this patch. I like how this is reviewable by just reading the added lines do exactly what the red line did, only in separate conditions, but if there is a strong preference for `Assert` I can do that here.
nit: front() could be UB. Not sure if we care about that, because there is a bunch of more UB in tests.
Could be one line shorter with ranges::equal?
Sure, seems fine to leave as-is. Just leaving a few comments, because if this was `BOOST_CHECK` (like in a few other places, see the comments), it would be UB.
I think one fix here would be to change the above check to `BOOST_REQUIRE`, but maybe in these cases I will migrate them to `Assert`?
I changed the some sites to `BOOST_REQUIRE` to stop the test before potential UB. Avoided `Assert` to not add more includes because it would be noisy for review.
Yeah, this is also a potential UB, it seems the ranges::equal fixed this.
The previous version made more sense since [`fresh` implies `dirty`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34864/changes/18e7474e37a2b86136a9d8e5856f5dd78c573109)

I'm not sure what you mean by "made more sense" because both checks are equivalent in this diff. If you are implying there is an invariant that should fail the test immediately, the second check can be converted to a `REQUIRE` if you prefer.
